title: N+1 Problem
description: Detect and fix the N+1 query pattern that kills application performance

data.text: The N+1 problem occurs when an application executes one query to fetch parent rows and then N additional queries to fetch related child rows. This multiplies round trips and database load.

data.title: Symptoms
items: Latency scales linearly with result set size

data.title: N+1 in application code
data.content: Looping over authors and querying books per author causes N+1 queries.

data.title: Fixed with JOIN
data.content: Use a single query with JOIN to eliminate N+1.
data.code:
SELECT a.author_id, a.name, b.title
FROM authors a
LEFT JOIN books b ON a.author_id = b.author_id
ORDER BY a.author_id;

data.title: Warning
data.text: ORMs with lazy loading are the most common source of N+1. Enable eager loading or query hints in your data access layer.

items.question: How do I detect N+1 in production?
items.answer: Enable query logging or APM tools that flag repeated similar queries in a single request.

items.question: Does COUNT always indicate N+1?
items.answer: No. COUNT alone is not enough. Look for repeated similar queries within the same request context.

items.question: Is IN better than JOIN?
items.answer: IN avoids Cartesian products but can be slower than JOIN on some databases. Test both.

data.title: Summary
points: N+1 multiplies queries by result set size
Replace loops with JOINs or batch queries
data.takeaway: N+1 is the most common ORM performance bug. One JOIN or batch query replaces N individual lookups.
